input:
Liquid-liquid extraction can be used to recover acetone from an aqueous stream into an organic solvent. The distribution coefficient of acetone, defined as the ratio between the organic and aqueous phases, is 1.93 at 25 °C, and the design is based on 8 countercurrent stages. On this basis, the predicted recovery is 95% of the acetone present in the feed.

The coefficient effectively determines the scale of the separation task: at a value of 1.93, each equilibrium contact transfers a majority of the acetone present toward the solvent phase, and the 8 countercurrent stages progressively compound that transfer along the column. The 95% recovery figure is the result of that staging under the two assumptions stated in the design. Firstly, the prediction assumes equilibrium stages, meaning that every stage is taken to reach the distribution described by the coefficient. Secondly, it assumes negligible mutual solubility, so that the aqueous and organic streams retain their identity from stage to stage and the coefficient measured for the pair remains applicable throughout. However, neither of these assumptions has been checked on the actual solvents. The equilibrium assumption may break down where contact time or dispersion in a real stage leaves the streams short of equilibrium, while the solubility assumption may break down where the actual solvent pair dissolves into each other sufficiently to shift the distribution. As a result, the 95% figure should be regarded as a prediction that rests on stated assumptions, with its two most important assumptions still untested on the solvents the design would actually run.
target:
Liquid-liquid extraction recovers acetone from an aqueous stream into an organic solvent. The distribution coefficient of acetone, organic over aqueous, is 1.93 at 25 °C, and the design uses 8 countercurrent stages. Predicted recovery is 95% of the acetone in the feed.

The coefficient sets the size of the task: at 1.93, each equilibrium contact moves a majority of the acetone present toward the solvent, and 8 countercurrent stages compound that movement along the column, each stage working on streams already enriched or depleted by the stages before it. The 95% recovery is the result of that staging under the design's two stated assumptions. The prediction assumes equilibrium stages: every stage is taken to reach the distribution the coefficient describes. It also assumes negligible mutual solubility, so the aqueous and organic streams keep their identity from stage to stage and the coefficient measured for the pair applies throughout. Neither assumption has been checked on the actual solvents. The equilibrium assumption fails where contact time or dispersion in a real stage leaves the streams short of equilibrium, and the solubility assumption fails where the actual solvent pair dissolves into each other enough to shift the distribution. The 95% figure therefore stands as a prediction under stated assumptions, with its two load-bearing assumptions untested on the solvents the design would run.
